quiz.title: Inverse Trig Exercise 2.2 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the properties used in Exercise 2.2 — complementary pairs, the double-angle forms, the addition formula and simplifying expressions. Answer each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 12 inverse trigonometric functions: properties and simplification

questions.q: For every x in [−1, 1], sin−¹x + cos−¹x equals:
questions.explanation: sin−¹x and cos−¹x are complementary, so their sum is π/2 for all x in the domain.
The double-angle result is 2 tan−¹x = tan−¹(2x/(1−x²)) when |x| < 1.
Using tan−¹x + tan−¹y = tan−¹((x+y)/(1−xy)): (1/2+1/3)/(1−1/6) = (5/6)/(5/6) = 1, so the sum is tan−¹1 = π/4.

questions.q: For 0 < x < π/2, tan−¹((cos x − sin x)/(cos x + sin x)) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by cos x to get (1−tan x)/(1+tan x) = tan(π/4 − x), so the value is π/4 − x.

questions.q: Written as a single inverse tangent, 2 tan−¹(1/3) equals:
For 0 < x < π, tan−¹(√((1−cos x)/(1+cos x))) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: (1−cos x)/(1+cos x) = tan²(x/2), so the square root is tan(x/2) and the expression equals x/2.

questions.q: The identity 3 sin−¹x = sin−¹(…) has which right-hand side?
questions.explanation: Since sin 3θ = 3 sinθ − 4 sin³θ, putting θ = sin−¹x gives 3 sin−¹x = sin−¹(3x − 4x³).

questions.q: The formula tan−¹x + tan−¹y = tan−¹((x+y)/(1−xy)) holds directly when:
questions.explanation: The addition formula applies as written when xy < 1; for xy > 1 a correction of ±π is needed.

faq.q: What does Exercise 2.2 of Inverse Trigonometric Functions cover?
faq.a: It focuses on the properties of inverse trigonometric functions — the complementary relations such as sin−¹x + cos−¹x = π/2, the double-angle forms of 2 tan−¹x, the addition formula for tan−¹x + tan−¹y, and using these to simplify or prove expressions.

faq.q: How is Exercise 2.2 different from Exercise 2.1?
faq.a: Exercise 2.1 is about finding principal values of a single inverse function. Exercise 2.2 assumes you know those and asks you to apply identities — combining, converting and simplifying inverse-trig expressions rather than reading a value off the unit circle.

faq.q: When can I use tan−¹x + tan−¹y = tan−¹((x+y)/(1−xy))?
faq.a: Use it directly only when xy < 1. If xy > 1 the true sum lies outside the principal range, so you add π (for positive x, y) or subtract π (for negative x, y) to correct it.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to simplify expressions like tan−¹(√((1−cos x)/(1+cos x)))?
faq.a: Convert to half-angle form. Here (1−cos x)/(1+cos x) = tan²(x/2), so the expression collapses to x/2. Recognising the half-angle and Pythagorean identities is the key skill in this exercise.
